source.title: Rethinking Learned Image Compression: Context is All You Need

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests parameter and dataset scaling in learned image compression and reports that simple backbone scaling does not keep improving performance, while context scaling can have non-monotonic effects. It presents these results as distinct from large-language-model scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper does not run language models or fit power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its own image-compression scaling and training-regime results bear on V5. Cited language-model scaling-law results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study scales parameters (encoder/decoder width M, context-model share) and training-set size in a learned image compression model and reports rate-distortion outcomes. That is a new setting with results bearing on V5, whether scaling behaviour carries over beyond text. It fits no power law, the ranges are narrow (8x width, 2x data), and it reports bpp and PSNR separately rather than a single loss, so the test is weak.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling learned image compression means scaling the context model and decoder, and that simply enlarging the backbone or the dataset does not keep improving compression. They add that overfitting serves as effective context but does not define LIC's limits. They also suggest CNNs may lack transformers' scaling-law properties and that image tokenization differs from text.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies an ELIC-based image-compression model, scaling its components and changing training data; it does not implement the language-model scaling-law recipe or fit its power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that outcomes vary with component being scaled, bit rate, training-data choice, model structure, and whether training overfits the Kodak evaluation data.

fits_no_version.finding: Overfitting the model on the Kodak test set greatly raises Kodak PSNR but generalizes poorly to CLIC2021.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-set overfitting acts as context in learned image compression; this concerns generalization, not scaling.

record.problems: No power-law curves or exponents are fitted; there is no compute-optimal allocation analysis. Some scaling conclusions rely on figures without numerical values in the text. Several comparisons use different bit rates, limiting direct comparison.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or exponent; scale ranges are under one order of magnitude. No video-model training, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. No single held-out loss (R+λD) is reported.
Language-model pretraining loss is not studied.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
No exponents or fitting choices are studied.

missing.what: Rate-distortion curves versus context-model channel number
Rate-distortion curves for the training-data ablation (8000 vs 16000 images, mixed, overfit); no numbers in the text

record.verdict_notes: Weak test. The paper takes LLM scaling laws only as motivation. Scale ranges are small, each setting is a single run with no uncertainty, and bpp/PSNR trade-offs make per-row direction ambiguous. The ELIC-based model is a CNN, which the authors flag as a possible reason scaling fails. Verdicts rest on Table 3, Table 4 and Section 4.4 text.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture details at fixed parameter count; the reported M sweep does not hold parameter count fixed.
The paper studies learned image compression, not other modalities such as video-model training, nor fine-tuning or transfer in language models. It does not fit or establish a power-law form.
Downstream task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, and their sensitivity to parameter counting or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: CNN-based (ELIC) learned image compression: backbone width scaled 192 to 1536, training data 8000 to 16000 images
relationships.reason: An 8x width increase gives no consistent rate-distortion gain (Table 3: r2-r4). Doubling the data gives no improvement on Kodak (r15). The range is narrow and no power law was fitted.
relationships.display_finding: An eightfold width increase produced no consistent rate-distortion gain, and doubling training data produced no improvement on Kodak.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: CNN-based (ELIC) learned image compression: backbone width scaled 192 to 1536, training data 8000 to 16000 images
source_check.reason: Table 3 shows no consistent rate-distortion improvement; Sections 4.4, 5.4 and 6 explicitly report negligible or absent gains from enlarging the dataset or backbone. This challenges continued beneficial scaling in these tested conditions, without establishing a general rejection of power laws.

relationships.condition: Scaling the context-model share (128 to 1280 GFLOPS settings)
relationships.reason: Rate-distortion improves up to 620 GFLOPS (r6-r7), then bpp keeps falling while PSNR drops (r8-r9). Gains are non-monotonic and the context share is confounded with backbone growth.
relationships.display_finding: Rate-distortion improved through 620 context channels, after which bitrate continued falling while PSNR declined.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Scaling the context-model share (128 to 1280 GFLOPS settings)
source_check.reason: The settings are context channel counts, not GFLOPS. More fundamentally, Table 4 reports two rate-distortion coordinates and Section 4.3 describes the later trade-offs as Pareto optimal. These trade-offs do not establish an incomplete or failed power-law form; no scalar scaling curve is fitted or tested for this condition group.

relation.reason: Its parameter and dataset sweeps, together with its explicit argument about limited scaling gains, bear on V5.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly investigates limits of transferring scaling laws to LIC and argues that increasing backbone parameters or training data does not continue improving compression. This is a specific qualification of V5, beyond introducing a new setting.

source_check.notes: Tables 3 and 4 designate no explicit baseline; their smallest settings can serve as analytical references. Power-law exponents and functional form remain untested; Table 3's caption names encoder and decoder, whereas Section 4.1 discusses encoder scaling.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Learned image compression parameter scaling and dataset-size scaling in the tested settings
reader_labels.reason: The results do not show a general, sustained power-law improvement: increasing backbone M gives little change, greater context share eventually lowers PSNR, and enlarging the training set has little effect (r1-r9, r15-r16).
